justification: Finding 0 identifies the same defect as the known bug. It says `part.match(_placeholderRe)` is "true for any placeholder, not just hex escapes" and notes that SafeSelector "also replaces attribute selectors". It gives `[a] .b` as an example where the separator is skipped and scoping breaks, and recommends restricting the check to hex-escape placeholders, which is exactly the fix. Finding 1 instead blames non-space combinators after a hex escape (`.\fc+bar`), not the placeholder being shared with attribute selectors, so it is a different mechanism.
ground_truth: To avoid treating the space in an escaped selector (".\fc ber") as a combinator, the PR skips a separator when the preceding part matches `_placeholderRe` (`__ph-N__`) and the next character is a hex digit. But SafeSelector uses the same `__ph-N__` placeholder for attribute selectors and other content, not only for escape sequences. In minified CSS without spaces, e.g. `:host[foo]>div`, the `>` separator is skipped because the part contains an attribute placeholder and the next char 'd' is hex, so the selector is scoped incorrectly and styles on :host attributes break in production builds. Fixed by giving escapes their own `__esc-ph-N__` placeholder and checking only for that.

findings.description: The skip condition is too broad. `part.match(_placeholderRe)` is true for any placeholder, not just hex escapes. SafeSelector also replaces attribute selectors (`[attr=x]`), `:nth-child(...)` arguments and non-hex escapes such as `\:`. If any of these precedes a real descendant space and the next compound starts with a hex-looking character (a-f or 0-9), the separator is skipped. Examples are `.hover\:bg-blue .bar`, `.md\:flex .container` and `[a] .b`. The two selector parts are then merged and only the last one is scoped, so the earlier part never gets the `[contenta]` attribute. This is a regression in view-encapsulation scoping. The check should be limited to placeholders that stand for a hex escape.

The lookahead uses `selector[res.index + 1]` for every separator type, but the separator regex also matches `+`, `~` and `>>>`. For a combinator without a following space, such as `.\fc+bar`, the char after the combinator is a hex char, so the combinator is wrongly treated as part of an escape sequence and skipped. The check is only meaningful when the separator is a literal space.

justification: Finding 0 identifies the same defect. It says `part.match(_placeholderRe)` matches any placeholder, including the ones SafeSelector creates for attribute selectors. As a result, a real combinator followed by a hex character is skipped and the selector is scoped wrongly. The examples use spaces rather than `>`, but the faulty code and the failure mechanism are the same.
ground_truth: To avoid treating the space in an escaped selector (".\fc ber") as a combinator, the PR skips a separator when the preceding part matches `_placeholderRe` (`__ph-N__`) and the next character is a hex digit. But SafeSelector uses the same `__ph-N__` placeholder for attribute selectors and other content, not only for escape sequences. In minified CSS without spaces, e.g. `:host[foo]>div`, the `>` separator is skipped because the part contains an attribute placeholder and the next char 'd' is hex, so the selector is scoped incorrectly and styles on :host attributes break in production builds. Fixed by giving escapes their own `__esc-ph-N__` placeholder and checking only for that.

findings.description: The check `part.match(_placeholderRe)` only tests whether the part contains any placeholder. It does not test that the part ends with an escaped character. SafeSelector also uses `__ph-N__` placeholders for attribute selectors such as `[hidden]` and for `:nth-child(...)` expressions. A real descendant combinator after one of these is then wrongly treated as an escape-terminating space whenever the next character is a hex digit or a letter a-f. Examples are `[hidden] div`, `[type=x] button` and `.a\:b .cd`. The separator is skipped and the two compound selectors are scoped as one part, so the first compound loses its `[contenta]` attribute. This changes the scoped output and can leak styles or alter specificity compared with before.

justification: Finding 0 identifies the same defect in test_hooks.ts. It says the guards `if (_global.beforeEach)` were removed, so `beforeEach(...)`/`afterEach(...)` are "called unconditionally at module load" and the module "throws a ReferenceError" in environments without a test framework. That is the same mechanism as the known bug. Finding 1 concerns matchers.ts, a different file and issue. Finding 2 is about the removed `ɵ_global` export, which is unrelated.
ground_truth: While replacing `global` with `globalThis`, the PR removed the guards around the Jasmine/Jest hooks in `@angular/core/testing` test_hooks.ts: `if (_global.beforeEach) {...}` became an unconditional `beforeEach(...)` / `afterEach(...)`. When this module is evaluated outside a test runner (e.g. it ends up in an application bundle), `beforeEach` is undefined and loading the module throws a ReferenceError. Fixed by calling `globalThis.beforeEach?.(...)` / `globalThis.afterEach?.(...)`.

findings.description: The `if (_global.beforeEach)` / `if (_global.afterEach)` guards were removed, so `beforeEach(...)` and `afterEach(...)` are now called unconditionally at module load. `@angular/core/testing` is imported in environments without a test framework, for example server-side code, utility scripts, or an import before jasmine/mocha is loaded. In those cases it now throws a ReferenceError. This is a regression for existing users, and the old guarded behavior was intentionally safe.

`beforeEach(...)` is now called unconditionally at module load, and `expect` is captured at that point. Without the previous `window`/`global` lookup and `_global.expect` access, importing this module where jasmine globals are not yet defined throws a ReferenceError. The module-level `expect as any` is also evaluated eagerly, so a framework that replaces `expect` later leaves the exported alias stale.

The `_global` export and its private re-export `ɵ_global` were removed from `@angular/localize`. This is a breaking change for any consumer or other package that imports `ɵ_global`, such as tooling or tests. Within this PR only `init` was updated, so other usages could fail to compile.

justification: Finding 0 points at the removed `if (_global.beforeEach)` / `if (_global.afterEach)` guards in test_hooks.ts. It says the now-unconditional calls throw "a ReferenceError at module load" when no test framework defines these globals. That is the same faulty code and the same failure mechanism as the known bug.
ground_truth: While replacing `global` with `globalThis`, the PR removed the guards around the Jasmine/Jest hooks in `@angular/core/testing` test_hooks.ts: `if (_global.beforeEach) {...}` became an unconditional `beforeEach(...)` / `afterEach(...)`. When this module is evaluated outside a test runner (e.g. it ends up in an application bundle), `beforeEach` is undefined and loading the module throws a ReferenceError. Fixed by calling `globalThis.beforeEach?.(...)` / `globalThis.afterEach?.(...)`.

findings.description: The old code guarded the hook registration with `if (_global.beforeEach)` and `if (_global.afterEach)`. The new code calls `beforeEach(...)` and `afterEach(...)` unconditionally. Importing `@angular/core/testing` where no test framework has defined these globals now throws a ReferenceError at module load. Examples are a bundler or tooling context, or a runner that only defines `beforeEach`. This is a behavior regression in a refactor labelled as having no functional changes.

justification: Finding [0] concerns the `isDefaultImport` heuristic misclassifying combined imports such as `import CmpA, {CmpB}`. The known bug is different: `deferBlockDep.isDefaultImport` is never assigned in `collectDeferredSymbols`, so it stays false even for pure default imports. Finding [0] does not identify the missing assignment and would not lead a maintainer to it, so it does not match.
ground_truth: The PR adds support for default imports in `@defer` dependencies and records `isDefaultImport` in the `deferrableTypes` map, but never sets `deferBlockDep.isDefaultImport` on the per-block dependency objects (they keep the initial `isDefaultImport: false`). The generated dependency loader function for the defer block reads that flag, so for a default-imported component it emits `m.ComponentName` instead of `m.default`, and loading the deferred block yields undefined. Fixed by setting `deferBlockDep.isDefaultImport = isDefaultImport(importDecl)` in `collectDeferredSymbols`.

findings.description: `isDefaultImport` returns true only when `importClause.namedBindings` is undefined. For a combined import such as `import CmpA, {CmpB} from './x'`, `namedBindings` is defined, so the default-imported `CmpA` is treated as a named import. The generated deferred loader then reads `m.CmpA` instead of `m.default`, which resolves to undefined at runtime. The check should also look at `importClause.name`. It also ignores type-only or other import clause forms, and it is true for a default import only by accident of the absent named bindings.

justification: The known bug is that `collectDeferredSymbols` never assigns `deferBlockDep.isDefaultImport`, so the per-block deps keep `false`. Finding [0] instead says the `isDefaultImport` helper misclassifies mixed imports such as `import CmpA, {Other}`. That is a different flaw in different logic, so it would not point a maintainer to the missing assignment on `deferBlockDep`.
ground_truth: The PR adds support for default imports in `@defer` dependencies and records `isDefaultImport` in the `deferrableTypes` map, but never sets `deferBlockDep.isDefaultImport` on the per-block dependency objects (they keep the initial `isDefaultImport: false`). The generated dependency loader function for the defer block reads that flag, so for a default-imported component it emits `m.ComponentName` instead of `m.default`, and loading the deferred block yields undefined. Fixed by setting `deferBlockDep.isDefaultImport = isDefaultImport(importDecl)` in `collectDeferredSymbols`.

findings.description: isDefaultImport only checks that `namedBindings === undefined`. For a mixed import such as `import CmpA, {Other} from './a'`, the default binding `CmpA` has `namedBindings` defined, so the function returns false. The generated dynamic import then uses `m.CmpA` instead of `m.default`, which resolves to undefined at runtime. The check also ignores which binding the deferred symbol actually comes from. For example, with `import Def, {Named}`, `Named` and `Def` get the same result.

justification: Finding 0 argues the default-handling clause is inverted and says links that "don't depend on router state subscribe needlessly". That is the explicitly excluded alternative: its fix would subscribe in fewer cases, not recognize that relative links always need the subscription. Finding 1 flags the inverted, dead constructor call and the resulting reliance on ngOnChanges. It does not identify that the subscription-skipping optimization itself is wrong because relative links' hrefs change with the ActivatedRoute on navigation.
ground_truth: RouterLink on anchor elements now only subscribes to router NavigationEnd events (to recompute `href`) when `subscribeToNavigationEventsIfNecessary` decides the link depends on router state, i.e. only for `preserveFragment` or `queryParamsHandling` 'merge'/'preserve' (plus a clause about the router's default handling). But the href of a relative link also changes whenever navigation changes the ActivatedRoute it resolves against. E.g. `<a [routerLink]="['./child']" queryParamsHandling="replace">` keeps showing `/initial/child` after navigating to `/different`. The optimization's premise is wrong, so hrefs go stale after navigation. The fix removes the condition and always subscribes for anchor elements (effectively rolling back the PR). A finding that only says the default-handling clause is inverted, and implies subscribing in fewer cases, is a different defect: its fix would remove subscriptions that relative links need, the opposite of the real fix.

findings.description: The condition for subscribing to NavigationEnd looks inverted. With no `queryParamsHandling` on the link, it subscribes only when the router's `defaultQueryParamsHandling` is not 'merge' or 'preserve'. So a link that relies on a router default of 'merge' or 'preserve' never subscribes, and its href goes stale after navigation. Meanwhile links that don't depend on router state subscribe needlessly.

The constructor calls `subscribeToNavigationEventsIfNecessary()` only when `!this.isAnchorElement`, but that method returns immediately for non-anchor elements. The call is dead code and the condition is inverted. Subscription for anchors now depends entirely on `ngOnChanges`, so an anchor that never gets `ngOnChanges` will never update its href on navigation.

justification: Finding 0 is about the constructor's `if (!isAnchorElement)` inversion and the resulting tabindex/accessibility problem. It does not identify that relative links need a NavigationEnd subscription whenever the ActivatedRoute changes. Finding 1 says only that the default-handling clause is backwards ("skips subscribing when the global default is 'merge' or 'preserve'"). The ground truth explicitly treats that as a different defect. Neither finding recognizes that the optimization's premise is wrong: relative links with 'replace' or no handling still go stale after navigation.
ground_truth: RouterLink on anchor elements now only subscribes to router NavigationEnd events (to recompute `href`) when `subscribeToNavigationEventsIfNecessary` decides the link depends on router state, i.e. only for `preserveFragment` or `queryParamsHandling` 'merge'/'preserve' (plus a clause about the router's default handling). But the href of a relative link also changes whenever navigation changes the ActivatedRoute it resolves against. E.g. `<a [routerLink]="['./child']" queryParamsHandling="replace">` keeps showing `/initial/child` after navigating to `/different`. The optimization's premise is wrong, so hrefs go stale after navigation. The fix removes the condition and always subscribes for anchor elements (effectively rolling back the PR). A finding that only says the default-handling clause is inverted, and implies subscribing in fewer cases, is a different defect: its fix would remove subscriptions that relative links need, the opposite of the real fix.

findings.description: The constructor condition is inverted. It was `if (isAnchorElement) { subscribe } else { setTabIndexIfNotOnNativeEl('0') }`. It is now `if (!isAnchorElement) { subscribeToNavigationEventsIfNecessary() } else { setTabIndexIfNotOnNativeEl('0') }`. The subscribe call returns immediately for non-anchor elements, so it does nothing. Anchor elements therefore get `tabindex=0` set and no NavigationEnd subscription from the constructor. Non-anchor elements such as `<div routerLink>` no longer get a default tabindex, which breaks keyboard accessibility.

The subscription condition for default query params handling looks backwards. `!this.queryParamsHandling && !dependsOnRouterState(options?.defaultQueryParamsHandling)` subscribes when the default does not depend on router state. It skips subscribing when the global default is 'merge' or 'preserve', which is exactly when the href depends on the current router state's query params. In that case the href goes stale after navigation.

justification: Finding 0 identifies the same mechanism. It notes that an observable that "completes without emitting used to resolve `undefined`, but now it rejects with `EmptyError`", which leads to unexpected errors in recognition (e.g., loadChildren). That is the same defect as the known bug: EmptyError from first() replaces toPromise's undefined. It doesn't specifically mention guards or matchers or the NoMatch catch, but it would lead a maintainer to the actual bug.
ground_truth: The PR replaces `.toPromise()` with a custom `firstValueFrom` (built on rxjs `first()`) in route recognition (`matchWithChecks`, `runCanLoadGuards`, `loadChildren`). Unlike `toPromise()`, which resolves `undefined` when an observable completes without emitting, `first()` errors with an EmptyError. Guards or matchers whose observables complete without emitting now throw EmptyError instead of being treated as "no match"; the recognizer's catch only skips NoMatch errors, so navigation fails instead of moving on to the next route. Fixed by also treating EmptyError as a non-match in recognize.ts.

findings.description: The helper replaces `toPromise()` with `first()`, which changes behavior in two ways. An observable that completes without emitting used to resolve `undefined`, but now it rejects with `EmptyError`. For example, a `redirectTo` function or `loadChildren` that returns `EMPTY` used to reach the `if (!cfg) throw canLoadFails(route)` handling, but now throws an unexpected `EmptyError`. An observable that emits several values before completing used to resolve with the last value (`toPromise` semantics), but now resolves with the first. Existing users of such observables could therefore see different results.

justification: Finding 0 describes the same defect as the known bug. It says `cancelLeavingNodes` "treats any leaving element in a different DOM parent as an overlay duplicate and force-removes it." It also notes that "`leavingNodes` is keyed by TNode... shared by every instance", so a distinct instance's leave animation "is cut short even though it is not a duplicate." This is the same mechanism as the known bug. Findings 1 and 2 describe different issues: a memory leak from stale tracking, and the removed queue cleanup.
ground_truth: `cancelLeavingNodes` now force-removes any element tracked as leaving for the same TNode whenever it sits in a different DOM parent than the newly inserted element (added to de-duplicate dynamic components re-rendered into a fresh overlay pane). `leavingNodes` is keyed by TNode, which is shared by every instance of a template, so distinct sibling instances (e.g. an accordion where opening section B collapses section A in another parent) are also "different parent": the still-animating element is removed synchronously and its `animate.leave` animation is skipped. Fixed by tracking the declaration view of each leaving element and only doing the cross-parent removal for the same logical view.

findings.description: cancelLeavingNodes treats any leaving element in a different DOM parent as an overlay duplicate and force-removes it. `leavingNodes` is keyed by TNode, and a TNode is shared by every instance of a component or template. If one instance is leaving in parent X while a new instance of the same component is inserted in parent Y (for example two list hosts, or a different place in the page), the leaving element is cancelled and removed immediately. Its leave animation is cut short even though it is not a duplicate.

trackLeavingNodes is now called on every Detach for any tNode that has a leave animation. It runs even when animations are disabled or the leave animation is skipped, and in that case clearLeavingNodes is never called. The element then stays in `leavingNodes` indefinitely. These stale, detached elements leak memory and are re-evaluated on every later insert. Moves that detach and re-insert a node are also tracked as leaving.

The code that removed pending enter animations from the animation queue when the same node is detached before the queue ran (removeAnimationsFromQueue) was deleted. Queued enter animations can now still run on an element that has already started its leave animation or been removed. This can cause conflicting enter and leave classes or listeners to fire on a leaving element, such as an `@if` toggled twice quickly within one change detection cycle.

justification: Finding 0 identifies the same defect. It quotes that `cancelLeavingNodes` "force-removes any leaving element under the same tNode whose parent differs" and notes that "A tNode is shared by every instance". It concludes that another instance elsewhere "cancels the first one's leave animation and removes it from the DOM immediately". This matches the known bug's mechanism and symptom. Finding 1 describes stale tracking on move or reorder, and finding 2 describes a removed enter-queue cleanup; both are different issues.
ground_truth: `cancelLeavingNodes` now force-removes any element tracked as leaving for the same TNode whenever it sits in a different DOM parent than the newly inserted element (added to de-duplicate dynamic components re-rendered into a fresh overlay pane). `leavingNodes` is keyed by TNode, which is shared by every instance of a template, so distinct sibling instances (e.g. an accordion where opening section B collapses section A in another parent) are also "different parent": the still-animating element is removed synchronously and its `animate.leave` animation is skipped. Fixed by tracking the declaration view of each leaving element and only doing the cross-parent removal for the same logical view.

findings.description: `cancelLeavingNodes` force-removes any leaving element under the same tNode whose parent differs from the new element's parent. A tNode is shared by every instance of a template or component, so unrelated instances in different DOM parents share it. For example, a component with `animate.leave` on its root is used in several containers. When one instance is removed and animating out, creating another instance elsewhere cancels the first one's leave animation and removes it from the DOM immediately. This is a regression that breaks leave animations in ordinary non-overlay layouts.

On every Detach where the tNode has leave animations, the element is tracked in `leavingNodes`. This happens before it is known that a leave animation will actually run, and it also covers detaches that are part of a move or reorder. The element is not cleared on the move path. A live, re-inserted node can therefore stay in `leavingNodes`, and a later insert whose previousSibling is that node would treat it as leaving. That would dispatch a cancel and call `removeChild` on a visible element. The stale entries are also never cleaned up, which leaks them.

The code that removed a node's pending enter animations from the animation queue when its leave animation starts is gone. An element toggled off before the queued enter animation flushes will still have the enter function run against an element that is leaving or already removed. That can apply stale enter classes or listeners to the leaving element and conflict with its leave animation.

justification: Finding 0 matches the known bug. It notes that `position` used to be serialized as "0,1,2" and is now sent as "[0,1,2]". It says the backend still parses the comma-separated format, so "view source and select DOM element would fail to find the node." It also points out that the receiving side was not updated. This is the same defect and the same mechanism as the known bug.
ground_truth: To escape code injected into the inspected page, the PR changes `findConstructorByPosition('${position}')` and `findDomElementByPosition('${position}')` to pass `stringifyAndEscape(position)`. `position` is an array, so it used to be serialized implicitly as a comma-separated string ("0,1,2"); now it is passed as a JSON array string ("[0,1,2]"). The backend that parses this serialized id still expects the comma-separated format, so "view source" and "select DOM element" from the component tree break. The fix updates the backend (component-tree.ts) to the new format; the PR changed the wire format without updating its consumer.

findings.description: The old code interpolated `position` (a number[]) into a string template, so the backend received the comma-separated form "0,1,2". `stringifyAndEscape(position)` now passes the JSON string "[0,1,2]" instead. The backend's `findConstructorByPosition` and `findDomElementByPosition` appear to parse positions with `split(',').map(parseInt)`. That would give NaN for "[0" and "2]", so view source and select DOM element would fail to find the node. This diff does not change the receiving side, so the format change breaks both operations. The same applies to `selectDomElement` on line 26.

justification: Finding 0 matches the known bug. It notes that the position array used to be serialized as a comma-joined string ('0,1,2') and is now sent as "[0,1,2]", while the receiving functions still parse the comma format. It names the same affected operations: "viewSource and selectDomElement would resolve the wrong node or fail". This is the same mechanism as the known bug: the wire format changed without updating its consumer.
ground_truth: To escape code injected into the inspected page, the PR changes `findConstructorByPosition('${position}')` and `findDomElementByPosition('${position}')` to pass `stringifyAndEscape(position)`. `position` is an array, so it used to be serialized implicitly as a comma-separated string ("0,1,2"); now it is passed as a JSON array string ("[0,1,2]"). The backend that parses this serialized id still expects the comma-separated format, so "view source" and "select DOM element" from the component tree break. The fix updates the backend (component-tree.ts) to the new format; the PR changed the wire format without updating its consumer.

findings.description: The old template interpolated the ElementPosition array as a comma-joined string, e.g. '0,1,2'. The receiving functions (findConstructorByPosition and findDomElementByPosition) most likely parse it with split(',') and parseInt. stringifyAndEscape now sends the literal string "[0,1,2]", so the first and last indices parse as NaN, because parseInt('[0') is NaN. As a result viewSource and selectDomElement would resolve the wrong node or fail. The diff does not change the receiving side to JSON.parse the argument.
